title: Act I, Scene IV
focus: the hidden mind behind a loyal face

teacherSummary.text: Malcolm reports that Cawdor died nobly, confessing his treason. Duncan reflects 'There's no art to find the mind's construction in the face' just as Macbeth enters. He thanks Macbeth and Banquo, then names Malcolm Prince of Cumberland, his heir. Macbeth, aside, sees Malcolm as a step he must 'o'erleap' and asks the stars to hide his 'black and deep desires.' Duncan will visit Macbeth's castle at Inverness.

context.history: Scottish kingship was not strictly hereditary at this time; naming Malcolm Prince of Cumberland made him heir and closed Macbeth's lawful path to the throne.

significance: Dramatic irony peaks: Duncan says faces cannot be read at the moment a new traitor walks in. Macbeth's 'Stars, hide your fires' begins the play's imagery of darkness covering crime.
discussionQuestions: Can you tell what someone is really thinking from their face? Give an example.
Where does irony appear in this scene, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this scene connect to the book's larger concern with masculinity, power and violence?

Is execution done on Cawdor? Are not
Those in commission yet return’d?
My liege,
They are not yet come back. But I have spoke
With one that saw him die: who did report
That very frankly he confess’d his treasons,
Implored your highness’ pardon and set forth
A deep repentance: nothing in his life
Became him like the leaving it; he died
As one that had been studied in his death
To throw away the dearest thing he owed,
As ’twere a careless trifle.
There’s no art
To find the mind’s construction in the face:
He was a gentleman on whom I built
An absolute trust.

anchorPassages.text:
My plenteous joys,
Wanton in fulness, seek to hide themselves
In drops of sorrow. Sons, kinsmen, thanes,
And you whose places are the nearest, know
We will establish our estate upon
Our eldest, Malcolm, whom we name hereafter
The Prince of Cumberland; which honour must
Not unaccompanied invest him only,
But signs of nobleness, like stars, shall shine
On all deservers. From hence to Inverness,
And bind us further to you.
The rest is labour, which is not used for you:
I’ll be myself the harbinger and make joyful
The hearing of my wife with your approach;
So humbly take my leave.
My worthy Cawdor!
Aside.
The Prince of Cumberland! that is a step
On which I must fall down, or else o’erleap,
For in my way it lies. Stars, hide your fires;
Let not light see my black and deep desires:
The eye wink at the hand; yet let that be,
Which the eye fears, when it is done, to see.

segments.script: Scottish kingship was not strictly hereditary at this time; naming Malcolm Prince of Cumberland made him heir and closed Macbeth's lawful path to the throne. Dramatic irony peaks: Duncan says faces cannot be read at the moment a new traitor walks in. Macbeth's 'Stars, hide your fires' begins the play's imagery of darkness covering crime. Imagery: "Stars, hide your fires; / Let not light see my black and deep desires." Watch for darkness and light: Night and darkness hide crimes; the Macbeths call on darkness to cover their deeds, and putting out a light marks murder.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “There’s no art / To find the mind’s construction in the face” slowly and put it in my own words: Speaking of the traitor Cawdor, Duncan says there is no art to find the mind's construction in the face. Next, craft. I notice the irony: he says this just before Macbeth, the next traitor, enters. The strongest word is “face”: it names the surface that hides a person's real thoughts. Then, effect. What does Duncan say about reading people's faces? My answer: Duncan says there is no art to read people's faces, because he trusted the traitor Cawdor; he is fatally wrong again, since he is about to give the same trust to Macbeth, who will murder him.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Ask: What words in this line stand out, and what do they suggest? Expected student answer: “Stars”, “fires” and “black and deep desires” stand out. Macbeth asks the light itself to go out so that no one, not even heaven, can see the wish he is hiding. Ask: How does this line connect to appearance and reality? Expected student answer: Macbeth has just knelt to Duncan as a loyal subject, and here he asks the stars to hide what he really wants, so the line sets a loyal face against a hidden, disloyal mind.
